content: Before initiating therapy with ZINACEF (cefuroxime), it is essential to thoroughly assess whether the patient has a history of hypersensitivity reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. This medication should be administered with caution to patients who are sensitive to penicillin. Antibiotics, including ZINACEF, should be used cautiously in patients with a history of any type of allergy, particularly drug-related allergies. If an allergic reaction to ZINACEF occurs, the drug must be discontinued immediately. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions may necessitate the use of epinephrine and other emergency interventions. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including ZINACEF. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A detailed medical history is crucial, as CDAD has been reported to occur up to two months after antibiotic administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation if clinically indicated. For severe cases of antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis caused by C. difficile, oral vancomycin is the treatment of choice. Other potential causes of colitis should also be evaluated. Although ZINACEF rarely causes kidney function abnormalities, renal status should be monitored during therapy, particularly in seriously ill patients receiving maximum doses. Cephalosporins should be used cautiously in patients receiving potent diuretics, as this combination may adversely affect renal function. In patients with transient or persistent renal insufficiency, the total daily dose of ZINACEF should be reduced to prevent high and prolonged serum antibiotic concentrations (refer to DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION). Prolonged use of ZINACEF, like other antibiotics, may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, necessitating close patient monitoring. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, including ZINACEF, should be prescribed cautiously in individuals with a history of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis. Nephrotoxicity has been reported when cephalosporins are administered concurrently with aminoglycoside antibiotics. In the treatment of meningitis, mild-to-moderate hearing loss has been reported in some pediatric patients treated with cefuroxime. Additionally, persistence of positive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures at 18 to 36 hours has been observed with cefuroxime injection and other antibiotic therapies, though the clinical significance of this finding is unclear. Cephalosporins, including ZINACEF, may be associated with reduced prothrombin activity. Patients at risk include those with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, prolonged antimicrobial therapy, or those stabilized on anticoagulant therapy. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and exogenous vitamin K should be administered as needed. ZINACEF should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections or for prophylactic indications. Prescribing this medication in the absence of such indications is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including ZINACEF, are only effective against bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections such as the common cold. Patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as prescribed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or failing to complete the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the risk of bacterial resistance, making future infections harder to treat. Patients should also be informed that diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics, which usually resolves after discontinuation of the drug. However, if watery or bloody stools occur (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even two or more months after completing the antibiotic course, they should contact their physician immediately. Cefuroxime, like other antibiotics, may alter gut flora, potentially reducing the reabsorption of estrogen and decreasing the efficacy of combined estrogen/progesterone oral contraceptives. False-positive results for glucose in the urine may occur with copper reduction tests (e.g., Benedict's or Fehling's solution or CLINITEST® tablets) but not with enzyme-based tests for glycosuria. False-negative results may occur with ferricyanide tests; therefore, glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods are recommended for determining blood plasma glucose levels in patients receiving ZINACEF. Cefuroxime does not interfere with serum and urine creatinine assays using the alkaline picrate method. Lifetime animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of cefuroxime have not been conducted. However, no mutagenic activity was observed in the mouse lymphoma assay or bacterial mutation tests. Positive results were obtained in an in vitro chromosome aberration assay, but in vivo micronucleus tests at doses up to 10 g/kg yielded negative results. Reproductive studies in mice at doses up to 3,200 mg/kg/day (3.1 times the maximum recommended human dose based on body surface area) showed no impairment of fertility. Cefuroxime is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Reproductive studies in mice and rabbits at doses up to 6.3 and 2.1 times the maximum recommended human dose, respectively, revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. As animal studies are not always predictive of human response, cefuroxime should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Cefuroxime is excreted in human milk; therefore, caution should be exercised when administering ZINACEF to nursing mothers. The safety and efficacy of ZINACEF in pediatric patients under three months of age have not been established. Accumulation of cephalosporins in neonates, leading to prolonged drug half-life, has been reported. In clinical studies, no significant differences in safety or efficacy were observed between elderly and younger patients. However, elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, which may increase the risk of toxic reactions. Dose adjustments and renal function monitoring are recommended in elderly patients (refer to DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION).
